cases.case_name: Davidson v. Davidson
cases.holding: Reversing partial summary judgment as to one reporter and affirming as to another, the court held that immunity for reporting suspected child abuse under I.C. § 16-1606 is decided by the court rather than a jury but must be resolved under the traditional summary-judgment standard, and that a genuine fact issue existed on whether one reporter acted in bad faith.
cases.quote: the traditional summary judgment standard applies in the context of liability of persons reporting instances of suspected child abuse

relevance.INP-01: The only retrieved Idaho appellate decision construing the reporting and immunity provisions, I.C. §§ 16-1605 to 16-1607, that govern a mandatory reporter's exposure.
relevance.INP-02: Applies the same good-faith immunity analysis to reports by private citizens who are not designated reporters.
relevance.INP-06: Establishes that serial or retaliatory reports lose immunity if the trier finds bad faith, the practical limit on anonymous or repeat hotline reporting.
relevance.INP-07: The reporter's hospital presentation of the child was part of the reporting course of conduct assessed for good faith.
relevance.INP-08: Supplies the two prerequisites any professional reporter must satisfy for immunity: knowledge, reason to know, or suspicion of abuse, plus a good-faith report.
relevance.INP-10: Frames what a court examines when a report is escalated into an investigation — the reporter's suspicion and motive at the time of the report.
relevance.DEC-01: Treble-damage liability under I.C. § 16-1607 for false reporting is the counterweight to a screening system that must absorb unfounded reports.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines the immunity that attaches to statements made in the course of the ensuing agency and law-enforcement investigation.
relevance.ACT-05: Statements in the reporter's sworn petitions for domestic-violence protection orders were analyzed as related to the abuse report for immunity purposes.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that New York's fair-preponderance standard for permanent-neglect terminations violated the Due Process Clause and that a State must support its allegations at a parental-rights termination proceeding by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: Sets the constitutional floor that Idaho courts apply when an agency finding is carried forward into a proceeding that can sever the parent-child relationship.
relevance.OUT-02: The federal source of Idaho's clear-and-convincing burden under I.C. § 16-2005, applied in every Idaho termination appeal in this set.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointed counsel for every indigent parent in a termination proceeding and left the appointment question to the trial court in the first instance, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: Marks the federal constitutional minimum for counsel in termination cases; Idaho's statutory right to counsel in Title 16 proceedings is more protective than this floor.

cases.case_name: Wallis v. Spencer
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment for the officers and the city, the court held that children may be seized from parents without prior judicial authorization only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury, that reasonable cause is a jury question, and that subjecting seized children to invasive medical examinations without judicial authorization or parental notification implicates the family's right to make medical decisions.
cases.quote: The right to family association includes the right of parents to make important medical decisions for their children

relevance.INP-03: Controls Ninth Circuit law when police, rather than a caseworker, take protective custody of a child on an uninvestigated third-party tip.
relevance.INP-12: States the exigency showing required before emergency protective custody may be taken without a court order.
relevance.DEC-04: The leading circuit statement of the warrant-or-imminent-danger rule that binds Idaho actors in a § 1983 suit.
relevance.ACT-06: Holds that examinations and medical decisions for a child in protective custody cannot displace parental authority without judicial authorization and notice.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the substantive standard and the jury-question rule that make an unlawful removal claim survive summary judgment.
relevance.INP-06: Warns that an uncorroborated tip from an unreliable source may not supply reasonable cause to seize a child.
relevance.INP-07: Invasive investigatory medical examinations of a seized child require judicial authorization and parental notification.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a social worker violated the family's Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights by removing children without a warrant where nothing in the record showed imminent danger of serious bodily harm during the few hours needed to obtain one, and that the law to that effect was clearly established.
cases.quote: there is no support at all in the record for the conclusion that the Rogers children were likely in imminent danger of serious bodily harm

relevance.INP-03: A referral acted on eighteen days later cannot supply the exigency that excuses a warrant.
relevance.INP-12: Ties emergency custody to danger arising within the time a warrant would take, not to generalized neglect concerns.
relevance.DEC-04: The controlling circuit formulation of the emergency-removal test that an Idaho caseworker's decision is measured against.
relevance.FAIL-02: Denies qualified immunity for a warrantless removal unsupported by imminent-danger evidence.

cases.case_name: Mabe v. San Bernardino County, Department of Public Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment for the social worker on the removal claim, the court held that exigency requires imminent danger of future harm and that a material fact question existed where the worker had interviewed the child days earlier and left her in the home.
cases.quote: imminent danger of future harm is required to show exigency

relevance.DEC-01: A worker who investigates and then leaves the child at home has, by her own conduct, negated the exigency she later claims.
relevance.DEC-02: Shows that the content and timing of the investigative interview itself determine whether a later warrantless removal is lawful.
relevance.DEC-04: Distinguishes probable cause to remove from the imminent-danger showing required to remove without a warrant.
relevance.FAIL-02: Delay between investigation and seizure is the strongest evidence that an ensuing removal was unlawful.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of the Parental Rights of Doe (2014-09)
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a stepparent-adoption termination petition, holding that although abandonment was proved, the petitioners failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that termination was in the children's best interests and that a stepparent's superior parenting cannot be the basis for termination.
cases.quote: The magistrate court correctly held that the decision to terminate a parent's parental rights cannot be based upon whether a stepparent would better fulfill parental responsibilities than the biological parent

relevance.DEC-03: A proved statutory ground does not carry the best-interests element; each must be proved separately by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.OUT-02: The leading recent Idaho statement that best interests is an independent clear-and-convincing element in every termination case.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows the Idaho Supreme Court affirming outright dismissal of a termination petition where the petitioner's proof failed.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of the Parental Rights of Jane (2013-15) Doe
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination on neglect grounds, holding that neglect is a question of fact to be established by clear and convincing evidence, that substantial and competent evidence supported the aggravated-circumstances finding, and that the mother's due-process challenge to being relieved of a case plan was inadequately argued.
cases.quote: Whether neglect has occurred is a question of fact to be established by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: States the Idaho evidentiary standard governing a finding of neglect under I.C. §§ 16-2002(3) and 16-1602.
relevance.ACT-02: An aggravated-circumstances finding lawfully ends the Department's duty to offer a reunification case plan.
relevance.INP-08: School-based observations of a dirty, hungry, chronically tardy child were part of the substantial evidence supporting neglect.
relevance.OUT-02: Confirms that appellate review is for substantial and competent evidence, not reweighing of the clear-and-convincing showing.

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe
cases.holding: The court vacated the termination judgment and remanded because the magistrate court applied an erroneous legal standard to each statutory ground, including by measuring the incarceration ground by the aggregate time served rather than the time likely to be served after the hearing.
cases.quote: As the magistrate court applied an erroneous legal standard to each ground that it relied upon to terminate Doe's parental rights, we vacate the judgment terminating Doe's parental rights

relevance.FAIL-01: The clearest Idaho example of appellate reversal of a termination for legal error, including criticism of a magistrate's practice of letting the State draft the findings.
relevance.OUT-02: Fixes the forward-looking construction of the incarceration ground in I.C. § 16-2005(1)(e).

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe
cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that the Department's reunification efforts and its placement choices are CPA requirements that are not relevant to whether the statutory grounds for termination are proved, and that the mother's due-process rights were protected by the clear-and-convincing burden at the termination trial.
cases.quote: those cases also demonstrate that such findings are irrelevant to termination proceedings because reasonable efforts are requirements under the CPA, not Idaho's parental-rights termination statute

relevance.ACT-01: Explains that a parent's agreement to a case plan and the Department's service offers arise under the CPA, not the termination statute.
relevance.ACT-02: Draws the line lawyers most often miss: reasonable-efforts findings belong to the CPA case and must be contested there, not on the termination appeal.
relevance.ACT-04: Records the Department's obligation to canvass relatives and its stated reasons for rejecting a grandparent guardianship.
relevance.OUT-01: Holds that dissatisfaction with reunification efforts does not defeat a termination supported by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.OUT-03: Recites the Department's permissible reasons for disfavoring a relative guardianship over adoption.
relevance.DEC-06: Illustrates the protective-supervision and stipulation path a CPA case can take before custody is vested.
relevance.INP-05: Shows how relatives who volunteer as placements are screened by the Department rather than by the court.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of the Parental Rights of Jane (2014-23) Doe
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights to an Indian child, holding that the ICWA active-efforts finding under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) need not be made by clear and convincing evidence, while the state-law grounds must be proved by clear and convincing evidence and the § 1912(f) finding beyond a reasonable doubt.
cases.quote: The ICWA also does not require that the finding with respect to active efforts be made by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.INP-11: The controlling Idaho authority on the burden of proof for ICWA active efforts once a case is identified as involving an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms the separate § 1912(e) clear-and-convincing finding required before an Indian child may be placed in foster care.
relevance.OUT-02: Sets out the layered ICWA and state burdens that a termination involving an Indian child must satisfy.

cases.case_name: Roe v. State, Department of Health & Welfare
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a grandmother's motion to intervene, holding that the CPA confers no conditional right to intervene, that permissive intervention under I.R.C.P. 24(b)(2) is inconsistent with the CPA, and that once the Department has legal custody it, not the court, decides where the child lives.
cases.quote: Once the Department has legal custody of a child under the CPA, the Department and not the court has the authority to determine where the child should live

relevance.INP-04: Describes the full CPA sequence from petition through adjudicatory hearing and disposition that a court-ordered referral enters.
relevance.INP-05: A relative who asks to take the child cannot become a party; her remedy is the ASFA right to be heard at reviews and hearings.
relevance.ACT-03: Establishes that placement authority follows legal custody, which is why placement disputes are not litigated as custody contests.
relevance.ACT-04: Holds that the 'least disruptive environment' language of the CPA is a reasonable-efforts mandate, not a relative-placement entitlement.
relevance.DEC-05: Explains the narrow scope of a CPA petition: protection of the child, not adjudication of competing custody claims.
relevance.DEC-06: Sets out the CPA's declared policy of preserving family unity and preferring care in the child's own home.
relevance.OUT-01: Confirms the court's retained but limited authority to approve or refuse return of the child to the home from which removal occurred.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of John Doe
cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment for the Department, the court held that prospective adoptive parents cannot adopt a child in the Department's legal custody without the Department's written consent under I.C. § 16-1504(1)(f), and that the merits of their petition are immaterial absent that consent.
cases.quote: The Department has the sole authority to withhold its permission from the prospective adoptive parents

relevance.ACT-04: Kin and foster caregivers must obtain the Department's written consent before they can convert a placement into a permanent legal status.
relevance.OUT-02: Identifies the statutory consent prerequisite that controls every CPA-originated adoption in Idaho.
relevance.OUT-03: Shows why families pursue guardianship: without Department consent, adoption is unavailable as a matter of law regardless of best interests.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of the Parental Rights of John Doe (2014-26)
cases.holding: The court vacated a termination judgment that rested solely on a murder conviction and sentence later vacated on appeal, and construed I.C. § 16-2005(1)(e) to require that the parent be serving a sentence and be likely to remain incarcerated for a substantial period of the child's remaining minority.
cases.quote: In context, the word "incarcerated" refers to someone who has been convicted of a crime and is serving a sentence of incarceration

relevance.OUT-02: The controlling Idaho construction of the incarcerated-parent ground, including the factors a court may weigh in measuring a substantial period.
relevance.FAIL-01: Demonstrates that a termination built on a collateral criminal judgment collapses when that judgment is vacated.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of Baby Boy Doe
cases.holding: On the second appeal in the same case, the court held that none of the mother's consents satisfied ICWA's formalities so the 1990 termination of her rights was invalid and she had standing, and that the ICWA active-efforts finding under § 1912(d) need not be proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
cases.quote: We hold that none of the consents to terminate parental rights complied with ICWA's statutory formalities, and that the order of June 1990 terminating the mother's parental rights is invalid

relevance.INP-11: Holds that ICWA's consent formalities in 25 U.S.C. § 1913(a) displace state law whenever they give the parent greater protection, per § 1921.
relevance.OUT-02: A voluntary relinquishment that does not meet ICWA's formalities is void and cannot support a later termination or adoption.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of Baby Boy Doe
cases.holding: The court reversed the trial court's ruling that ICWA did not apply, vacated the termination order, and rejected the judicially created 'existing Indian family' exception, holding that ICWA governs the termination and placement of an Indian child regardless of whether the child was removed from an Indian home.
cases.quote: Limiting ICWA to situations in which an Indian child is being removed from an existing Indian family is, therefore, a judicially created exception to ICWA

relevance.INP-11: Idaho's foundational holding that ICWA is triggered by the child's status, not by the family's living arrangements.
relevance.ACT-03: ICWA's placement and evidentiary provisions attach to foster placement of an Indian child even when the child never lived in an Indian home.
relevance.ACT-04: Confirms that ICWA's placement preferences and tribal notice and intervention rights apply to the placement decision itself.

cases.case_name: State v. Doe
cases.holding: The court vacated a termination order and remanded, holding that the rebuttable presumption in I.C. § 16-1629(9) favors only the Department's filing of a termination petition after fifteen of twenty-two months in care and does not shift to the parent the burden of disproving that termination is in the child's best interests.
cases.quote: It does not create a presumption that it is in the best interests of the child to terminate parental rights

relevance.DEC-05: Correctly limits the ASFA-derived fifteen-of-twenty-two-month trigger to the decision whether to file a petition.
relevance.ACT-02: A parent's failure to complete services within the statutory window does not convert into a presumption against the parent at trial.
relevance.OUT-01: Preserves Idaho's longstanding presumption that a natural parent should have custody of his children.
relevance.OUT-02: Misallocating the burden of proof on best interests is structural error requiring a new termination trial.
relevance.FAIL-01: A leading Idaho reversal: applying the incorrect burden 'infected the trial' and was not harmless.

cases.case_name: Wade v. Taylor
cases.holding: Vacating the district court's disclosure order and remanding, the court held that public records are presumed open, that exemptions are narrowly construed, and that the withholding agency bears the burden of demonstrating a reasonable probability that disclosure would cause a harm listed in I.C. § 9-335(1).
cases.quote: this Court presumes the records to be open to the public, unless it is shown that an exemption applies

relevance.INP-09: Sets the evidentiary burden an oversight requester must force an Idaho agency to carry before records are withheld.
relevance.PMC-02: Investigatory and enforcement records may be withheld only on a record-specific, reasonable-probability showing, not a categorical one.
relevance.PMC-05: The controlling Idaho Public Records Act framework for any FOIA-style request to a state child-welfare agency.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines what an accountability project can lawfully demand and what an agency must prove to refuse.
relevance.FAIL-06: An agency that withholds without a thorough, record-specific justification has failed its statutory disclosure burden.

cases.case_name: State v. Barrett
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a suppression motion, holding that exigent circumstances justified a warrantless entry into a home where officers reasonably believed a wife and children inside might need emergency medical assistance, and that evidence in plain view during legitimate emergency activity may be seized.
cases.quote: The risk of danger to police officers or other persons either inside or outside the dwelling constitutes such an exigency justifying a warrantless entry

relevance.INP-03: The Idaho rule officers rely on when a welfare call escalates into entry and a child-protection referral.
relevance.INP-12: Idaho's own statement of the exigency and emergency-aid exception that underlies protective custody entries.
relevance.DEC-04: Anchors the state-law side of the warrantless-entry analysis that pairs with the Ninth Circuit's removal cases.
relevance.ACT-06: Entry to render emergency medical assistance to persons believed to be inside a dwelling is lawful without a warrant.

cases.case_name: D.A.F. v. Lieteau
cases.holding: Reversing the district court, the court held that the Idaho Tort Claims Act notice requirement applies to tort claims brought under the child-abuse claims statute, I.C. § 6-1701, while whistleblower claims under I.C. § 6-2101 et seq. are statutory actions outside the ITCA.
cases.quote: We hold that because of the plain language of the ITCA, the notice requirement applies to claims based on tort actions in child abuse cases

relevance.OUT-06: Sets the procedural gate — ITCA notice — that a family must clear before suing the State over harm to a child in its care.
relevance.FAIL-04: The Idaho Supreme Court's controlling ruling on suits arising from abuse of children held in state institutions.
relevance.FAIL-05: Holds that Idaho whistleblower claims are not subject to the ITCA, preserving a retaliation remedy for those who report agency misconduct.
relevance.FAIL-06: Protects the statutory whistleblower route by which internal agency failures reach the public record.
relevance.PMC-04: Defines the litigation channel through which serious-injury and fatality cases can be pursued and documented in Idaho.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' provision of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by private plaintiffs, either directly under the Act or through 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

relevance.INP-09: Explains why systemic child-welfare deficiencies are addressed through federal administrative oversight rather than private suit.
relevance.PMC-01: The reason CFSR findings and reasonable-efforts requirements are enforced by HHS, not by families in court.
relevance.PMC-02: Federal fiscal conditions on Title IV-E funds run to the agency and the Secretary, not to individual beneficiaries.
relevance.PMC-03: Statutory state-plan obligations such as citizen review are enforced through the plan-approval process, not litigation.
relevance.PMC-05: Confirms that transparency and compliance pressure must come from oversight and disclosure, not private enforcement.
relevance.PMC-06: The doctrinal basis for treating federal compliance failures as a monitoring and reporting problem rather than a justiciable one.
relevance.FAIL-03: Directly holds that a state's failure to meet the federal reasonable-efforts condition is not privately actionable.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a state to protect a child from private violence, so social workers who received abuse reports and failed to remove the child did not deprive him of liberty by their inaction.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.INP-01: Establishes that a report received and not acted on does not by itself create federal constitutional liability.
relevance.INP-02: Fixes the constitutional consequence of an agency's failure to act on third-party reports of abuse.
relevance.INP-08: A school's or professional's report that is logged but not acted on creates no federal duty running to the child.
relevance.DEC-01: The controlling authority limiting constitutional liability for a decision to screen out or close a report.
relevance.OUT-06: Frames why fatality cases against agencies must be pleaded as custody or state-created-danger claims, not failure-to-protect.
relevance.FAIL-04: The starting point — and the principal obstacle — for any claim arising from a child's death while known to the agency.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality prevention is pursued through review commissions and legislation rather than constitutional litigation.

cases.case_name: Palmore v. Sidoti
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed a custody change premised on the mother's interracial remarriage, holding that the effects of private racial prejudice cannot justify a racial classification removing a child from a parent found otherwise fit.
cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect

relevance.ACT-03: Bars an agency or court from treating anticipated community reaction to a child's race as a placement justification.
relevance.ACT-04: Race cannot be used as a reason to prefer or reject a relative or kinship home.
relevance.FAIL-05: The controlling constitutional rule against race-based placement and custody decisions in child welfare.

cases.case_name: Henry A. v. Willden
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Reversing dismissal in substantial part, the court held that foster children stated substantive due process claims under both the special-relationship and state-created-danger doctrines, and separately analyzed which Child Welfare Act and CAPTA provisions create rights enforceable under § 1983.
cases.quote: we have already held that the state-created danger doctrine applies to placing a foster child in a home where there is a known danger of abuse

relevance.ACT-03: Placing a child in a home despite known abuse reports is itself an actionable state-created danger.
relevance.ACT-06: Recognizes that deliberate indifference to a foster child's serious medical needs violates due process.
relevance.OUT-04: Analyzes which Title IV-E case-plan and case-review guarantees for children in care are enforceable under § 1983.
relevance.OUT-06: Applies both special-relationship and state-created-danger theories to systemic harm in a county foster system.
relevance.FAIL-03: Shows the narrow set of Child Welfare Act provisions that survive Suter and Blessing as privately enforceable rights.
relevance.FAIL-04: Holds that state officials retain supervisory responsibility even where foster care is administered by a county.
relevance.PMC-01: Confirms that state oversight of a devolved child-welfare system is itself a source of potential liability and accountability.

cases.case_name: Patterson v. State, Department of Health & Welfare
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the Department, holding that although the Idaho Human Rights Act prohibits retaliation against employees who oppose unlawful discrimination, complaints about an intra-office romance and paramour favoritism could not reasonably be believed to be protected activity.
cases.quote: The IHRA not only prohibits discriminatory actions against persons in protected groups, but also prohibits retaliation against persons who oppose such actions

relevance.FAIL-05: The Idaho Supreme Court's statement of the retaliation cause of action available against the Department under I.C. § 67-5911, and its limits.
relevance.FAIL-06: Marks the boundary of protected internal opposition for an agency employee who wants to surface misconduct.
relevance.PMC-05: Relevant to whether agency insiders can lawfully be sanctioned for the complaints that generate public disclosure.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of Copenhaver
cases.holding: The court reversed a permanent guardianship to non-relatives, holding that a court may reach the best-interests question only after finding the parent's rights terminated or suspended by circumstances under I.C. § 15-5-204, and that those circumstances had ceased once the mother appeared and objected.
cases.quote: "Suspended by circumstances" must contemplate some set of circumstances which deprives a parent of the ability to accept the rights and responsibilities of parenthood

relevance.INP-05: Shows that a non-parent's petition cannot displace a willing, available parent merely because the child is doing well elsewhere.
relevance.OUT-03: The controlling Idaho two-step for minor guardianships, and the parental presumption that must be overcome first.

cases.case_name: Wood v. State, Department of Health & Welfare
cases.holding: The court affirmed an order placing three children in permanent foster care until age eighteen, holding that a magistrate need not make a threshold determination limiting the CASA guardian ad litem's participation because I.C. § 16-1632(a) gives the guardian ad litem all the rights of a party, and that any evidentiary error was harmless.
cases.quote: which vests the guardian ad litem with all the rights of a party to a lawsuit

relevance.INP-04: Describes the court's own appointment of a CASA volunteer and the scope of participation that appointment carries.
relevance.DEC-05: Shows a guardian ad litem's termination petition being treated as a CPA modification motion, and how the resulting hearing proceeds.
relevance.ACT-03: The retrieved Idaho decision approving long-term foster care as the disposition where children's special needs required it.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanent foster care is an available Idaho permanency outcome distinct from guardianship or adoption.
relevance.OUT-04: The permanency order ran until the children reached eighteen, marking the statutory horizon of CPA foster care.
relevance.PMC-03: Illustrates the citizen-volunteer CASA role that Idaho relies on for independent review of individual cases.

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. John Doe and Jane Doe (2023-22)
cases.holding: The court denied further extensions and dismissed the parents' appeal under Idaho Appellate Rule 21 for failure to file the opening brief by the court-ordered deadline, and referred counsel to the Idaho State Bar.
cases.quote: The fact that counsel for Parents is a solo practitioner and encountered formatting problems is not an excuse

relevance.OUT-05: The parents' underlying claim that the child protective proceeding was groundless and arbitrary was never reached on the merits.
relevance.FAIL-01: The sharpest available warning that Idaho child-protective appeals are dismissed for missed briefing deadlines regardless of the merits.

cases.case_name: Blessing v. Freestone
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a state's obligation to operate a federally funded program in 'substantial compliance' with its plan is not intended to benefit individual beneficiaries and creates no enforceable right, and that courts must examine each statutory provision separately rather than take a blanket approach.
cases.quote: The Court of Appeals erred not only in finding that individuals have an enforceable right to substantial compliance

relevance.INP-09: Systemic performance shortfalls identified by federal audit are addressed by the funding agency, not by individual suit.
relevance.PMC-01: Directly on point: substantial-compliance standards of the CFSR type are monitoring tools, not individual entitlements.
relevance.PMC-02: Confirms that the remedy for audit-identified noncompliance is a federal corrective-action and funding process.
relevance.PMC-03: State-plan assurances such as citizen review panels are structural obligations owed to the Secretary.
relevance.PMC-06: Requires provision-by-provision analysis before any federal child-welfare requirement is treated as enforceable.
relevance.FAIL-03: The governing framework for what a state's failure to meet federal performance standards legally means.

cases.case_name: John Doe v. Jane Doe
cases.holding: The court dismissed an aunt's appeal from an adjudicatory order vesting protective custody of six children in the Department, holding that because she stipulated at the hearing that Department custody was in the children's best interests she preserved no error and presented no justiciable controversy.
cases.quote: When a litigant stipulates to the entry of an order, it renders an appeal of that order nonjusticiable as moot

relevance.INP-05: A relative caregiver who participates in the adjudicatory hearing must object on the record to preserve any placement challenge.
relevance.INP-12: Records the officer's declaration of imminent danger that initiated protective custody of the six children.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows that stipulated CPA dispositions are effectively unreviewable, which shapes how such cases end.
relevance.FAIL-01: Explains the preservation rule that defeats most Idaho appeals from child-protective dispositions.

cases.case_name: Turner v. Turner
cases.holding: The court affirmed a protection order obtained by a mother for herself and her son, declining to disturb Ellibee and holding that the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard remains the burden of proof under the Domestic Violence Crime Prevention Act despite longer order durations and firearm consequences.
cases.quote: The burden of proof under the DVCPA is preponderance of the evidence

relevance.ACT-05: The controlling Idaho authority on the standard of proof for a protective order that restrains contact with a child.
relevance.INP-03: Confirms that a civil protection order, obtainable on a preponderance, is an alternative to removal when safety can be secured by restraining the abuser.

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. John Doe (2023-25)
cases.holding: Affirming a redisposition order removing five children from a home that had been under protective supervision, the court held for the first time that a redisposition hearing under I.C. § 16-1623 is governed by the same preponderance-of-the-evidence standard as an adjudicatory hearing and does not unconstitutionally interfere with parental rights.
cases.quote: The redisposition hearing process is, in essence, another adjudicatory hearing resulting in a "redisposition" of the child's custody

relevance.INP-01: The case began with reports of physical abuse and neglect that produced a court-ordered investigation.
relevance.INP-02: Shows how reports from multiple sources are consolidated into a single court-ordered child-protective investigation.
relevance.INP-03: Documents the coordinated law-enforcement and Department response that preceded the CPA petition.
relevance.INP-04: The clearest recent Idaho example of a court ordering the Department to investigate and opening a protective-supervision case.
relevance.INP-10: Traces the escalation from screening and investigation to protective supervision and then to removal.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that a child under protective supervision may be removed without a prior hearing only if a redisposition hearing follows within 48 hours.
relevance.DEC-02: Describes the court-ordered investigation that follows acceptance of a report under the CPA.
relevance.DEC-03: Confirms that the CPA jurisdictional finding is made on a preponderance under I.C. § 16-1619(4), not clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.DEC-04: The controlling Idaho authority on the standard and procedure for removal of a child already under protective supervision.
relevance.DEC-05: Sets out the disposition options available once a petition is sustained, including protective supervision short of Department custody.
relevance.DEC-06: Protective supervision with the parents retaining custody is Idaho's statutory alternative to vesting legal custody in the Department.
relevance.ACT-01: Records the Department's safety plan and the parents' voluntary participation before the court departed from it.
relevance.ACT-03: Explains the best-interests and contrary-to-welfare findings required before legal custody is vested in the Department.
relevance.OUT-04: Notes that protective supervision may run for an indeterminate period not to exceed the child's eighteenth birthday.
relevance.FAIL-02: Holds that a redisposition supported by substantial and competent evidence is not an unconstitutional interference with parental rights.

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe (2016-11)
cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that the Department satisfied I.C. § 16-1621(3)(c) by developing four case plans identifying the issues, the parent's tasks and the Department's own role, and that substantial and competent evidence supported the findings of neglect, inability to discharge parental responsibilities, and best interests.
cases.quote: We hold that the magistrate court did not err by finding that the IDHW made reasonable efforts to reunify Mother with her children

relevance.ACT-02: Specifies what an adequate Idaho case plan must contain: the issues, the parent's tasks, and the Department's stated role.
relevance.OUT-01: The leading Idaho application of the CPA reasonable-reunification-efforts requirement in I.C. § 16-1621(3)(c).

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Hays
cases.holding: Affirming the district court's reversal of the magistrate, the court held that where parental rights have been terminated and the Department is appointed guardian of the child's person, the Department alone must consent to an adoption and therefore alone selects the adoptive parents, subject only to the adoption court's power to deny a petition that is not in the children's best interests.
cases.quote: The authority to consent to the adoption of a child necessarily includes the authority to decide who can be the adoptive parents.

relevance.ACT-04: Establishes that once parental rights are terminated and the Department is made guardian, kin and foster caregivers cannot convert a placement into adoption without the Department's consent.
relevance.OUT-02: The originating Idaho holding that the Department alone consents to, and therefore selects, the adoptive parents for a child in its guardianship — the rule In re Adoption of John Doe later applies.
relevance.OUT-03: Holds that the court may sanction a permanent placement other than adoption and must hold annual future-status hearings until one exists, which is the statutory space guardianship and long-term care occupy.

cases.case_name: Roe Family Services v. Doe
cases.holding: The court reversed a magistrate's decree terminating an unmarried biological father's parental rights and remanded, holding that although the magistrate's factual findings were supported by substantial and competent evidence he failed to apply the correct law, because a father who had filed a notarized acknowledgment of paternity with the mother's consent was entitled to notice of the termination hearing under I.C. §§ 16-2007 and 16-1505(1)(d).
cases.quote: The magistrate judge's factual findings are supported by substantial and competent evidence, but he failed to apply the correct law to the facts of this case.

relevance.FAIL-01: The Idaho Supreme Court's canonical statement that a magistrate's findings may be fully supported by the evidence and the termination still reversed because he applied the wrong law.
relevance.OUT-01: Reverses the termination and directs that custody and visitation be arranged for the biological father, applying Idaho's presumption that a natural parent should have custody as against non-parents.

cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe
cases.holding: Affirming termination as to both parents, the court held that I.C. § 16-1624 authorizes the Department to petition for termination once the court has found CPA jurisdiction at the adjudicatory hearing and placed the child in the Department's legal custody or protective supervision, so neither due process nor the termination statute's purpose provision requires that the parent first be given a full opportunity to complete a case plan.
cases.quote: Thus, under the authority granted by the CPA, the Department is authorized to petition for termination if the court has jurisdiction over the child under the CPA

relevance.ACT-02: Rejects the argument that a parent must first be given a full opportunity to complete a CPA case plan before the Department may petition to terminate.
relevance.OUT-01: Holds that the CPA's reunification framework does not condition the Department's termination petition, so dissatisfaction with reunification efforts is not by itself a defense to termination.
relevance.DEC-05: Identifies I.C. § 16-1624 as the statutory authority for filing a termination petition once CPA jurisdiction is found at the adjudicatory hearing.
relevance.FAIL-05: Separately holds that neither the CPA nor the termination statute obliges the Department to notify a parent of her disabled status; her statutory right is to present adaptive-equipment and supportive-services evidence.

cases.case_name: Idaho Dep't of Health & Welfare v. Doe (In Re Doe)
cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that substantial and competent evidence supported the magistrate's findings that the mother neglected her three children under both I.C. §§ 16-1602(31) and 16-2002(3)(b) and that termination was in the children's best interests, restating that due process requires the State to prove a statutory ground and best interests by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: a parent-child relationship may be terminated if the parent has neglected the child and it is in the child's best interest to terminate the relationship

relevance.DEC-03: The cleanest recent Idaho statement of the two-part termination test — a statutory ground plus best interests — each proved by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.OUT-02: The current Idaho articulation of what the State must prove to terminate, quoted in later decisions including IDHW v. John Doe (2023-25).

cases.case_name: Ellibee v. Ellibee
cases.holding: Affirming a ninety-day protection order obtained by a mother on behalf of her minor children, the court held that the Domestic Violence Crime Prevention Act may be used to obtain a protection order in favor of a child even against a parent holding joint legal custody, and that the standard of proof in such proceedings is preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: the required standard of proof in protection order proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act is the preponderance of the evidence

relevance.ACT-05: The originating Idaho holding that a DVCPA protection order restraining a parent's contact with a child issues on a preponderance of the evidence — the rule Turner v. Turner later declined to disturb.

cases.case_name: Van v. Portneuf Medical Center
cases.holding: Vacating summary judgment on the whistleblower count and remanding, the court held that a claim under Idaho's Protection of Public Employees Act is purely a statutory remedy against governmental employers and is therefore not subject to the Idaho Tort Claims Act notice requirement, while affirming dismissal of the contract-based claims.
cases.quote: Therefore, the district court erred in holding that compliance with the notice provision in Idaho Code section 6-906 was a prerequisite to bringing suit under the Whistleblower Act

relevance.FAIL-05: The actual Idaho holding that a whistleblower retaliation claim against a governmental employer is a statutory action exempt from the ITCA notice requirement.
relevance.FAIL-06: Preserves the practical route by which an agency insider can litigate retaliation for reporting waste or unlawful conduct without first serving an ITCA notice.
relevance.PMC-05: Protects the employee-disclosure channel that often supplies the documents and allegations an outside transparency request later seeks.

cases.case_name: Bolger v. Lance
cases.holding: Affirming denial of a public-records petition, the court held that Idaho public records are presumed open and exemptions narrowly construed, that the agency responding to an order to show cause bears the burden of persuasion to prove an exemption applies, and that the Attorney General carried that burden here through in camera review of the withheld investigatory records.
cases.quote: the agency bears the burden of persuasion and must "show cause," or prove, that the documents fit within one of the narrowly-construed exemptions

relevance.PMC-05: Allocates the burden in an Idaho public-records suit: the withholding agency must show cause and prove the records fit a narrowly construed exemption.
relevance.FAIL-06: The authority a requester cites when an agency asserts an exemption without proving it, and the case Wade v. Taylor relies on for that burden allocation.
relevance.INP-09: Shows how far an oversight requester can press: the agency must justify withholding, though in camera review of the documents themselves can satisfy that burden.
relevance.PMC-02: Confirms that the investigatory-records exemption reaches only records of an ongoing law-enforcement investigation and must be proved record by record.

cases.case_name: Federated Publications, Inc. v. Boise City
cases.holding: The court held that the names and resumes of applicants for appointment to a city council are not exempt personnel records because a council member is a local governmental official rather than an employee, and that a police department's administrative review of an officer-involved incident is not an exempt personnel record or performance evaluation, because exemptions to the open-records presumption are narrowly construed.
cases.quote: In deciding that the administrative review must be disclosed, we are also influenced by the presumption that all public records are open unless expressly provided otherwise by statute

relevance.PMC-05: The foundational Idaho Public Records Act decision establishing that all public records are presumed open and that exemptions are narrowly construed.
relevance.INP-09: Supplies the presumption of openness an oversight body or journalist invokes against a state agency's categorical refusal to produce.
relevance.FAIL-06: Holds that an agency's internal administrative review of its own personnel's conduct is not automatically an exempt personnel record or performance evaluation.
relevance.PMC-06: Requires exemption-by-exemption analysis of each withheld record rather than a blanket claim of confidentiality.

cases.case_name: State v. Pearson-Anderson
cases.holding: Affirming denial of a suppression motion, the court held that a warrantless entry into a home is presumed unlawful unless an exception applies, and that the exigent-circumstances exception justified an officer's brief entry after a 911 hang-up call where responding officers found two people fighting and had reason to believe another person inside might need assistance.
cases.quote: an officer's warrantless entry into a home is presumed to be unlawful unless it falls within a well-recognized exception

relevance.INP-12: Idaho's own statement that a warrantless entry into a home is presumptively unlawful — the baseline any emergency protective-custody entry must overcome.
relevance.DEC-04: The decision State v. Barrett applies for Idaho's exigency test, and therefore the originating state-law anchor of the warrantless-entry analysis.
relevance.INP-03: Holds that officers responding to a 911 hang-up call need not accept an on-scene explanation that all is well before checking the home for other persons.
relevance.ACT-06: Permits a brief warrantless entry for the limited purpose of determining whether a third person inside the dwelling needs emergency assistance.

notes: Method: every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read in full or in the relevant sections. Every quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after normalizing whitespace and curly quotation marks, and each was checked to fall in the majority (or per curiam) opinion body rather than a syllabus, headnote, concurrence or dissent.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the ID files are keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations ('IDHW v. Jane Doe', 'State v. John Doe, a juvenile', etc.). None of them survived retrieval and verification; none is carried forward here.

Idaho anonymizes all Child Protective Act and termination parties as 'Doe' or 'Roe'. Case names in this jurisdiction are therefore non-distinctive and several unrelated cases share the caption 'Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe'. Always resolve an Idaho child-welfare citation by cluster_id and reporter citation, never by case name.

OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out): no published Idaho appellate decision could be found on extended foster care, the Chafee program, independent-living services, or juvenile-court jurisdiction continuing past age 18. Searches for 'extended foster care', 'Chafee', 'independent living', and age-21 foster youth in the Idaho Supreme Court and Court of Appeals returned zero on-point results. The node is therefore served by the two Idaho decisions that fix the age-18 ceiling of CPA custody (Wood v. State; IDHW v. John Doe (2023-25), citing I.C. s 16-1619(5)(a)) plus the Ninth Circuit's Title IV-E case-plan and case-review analysis in Henry A. v. Willden. A practitioner should expect this question to be one of first impression in Idaho.

DEC-03 (Substantiated Finding): no Idaho appellate decision could be found construing a child protection central registry, an administrative appeal from a substantiated finding, or a Mathews v. Eldridge due-process challenge to such a finding. Searches for 'central registry' returned nothing in either Idaho court. The node is served by the burden-of-proof and neglect-definition cases and by Santosky's federal floor. Idaho's CPA route to court is the preponderance standard of I.C. s 16-1619(4) (IDHW v. John Doe (2023-25)); the clear-and-convincing standard attaches only at termination.

Fourth Amendment / caseworker conduct: Idaho's own appellate courts have not published a decision on warrantless entry by a child-protective caseworker, on in-school interviews of a child by CPS, or on s 1983 liability for wrongful removal. The governing law for Idaho actors is therefore Ninth Circuit: Wallis, Mabe, Rogers and the en banc Kirkpatrick. State v. Barrett supplies Idaho's own exigency and emergency-aid formulation but arises in a criminal-suppression posture. Greene v. Camreta, the Ninth Circuit's in-school-interview decision, was vacated as moot by the Supreme Court in Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011), and is deliberately not cited here; the in-school interview question is open in this circuit.

Wallis v. Spencer date: CourtListener records 14 September 1999 as the filing date for the cluster reported at 202 F.3d 1126, which is the opinion as amended on denial of rehearing (conventionally cited as 9th Cir. 2000). The date_decided and year fields reflect CourtListener's recorded date; the citation reflects the reporter. The superseded original opinion appears at 193 F.3d 1054.

The two ICWA decisions styled 'In the Matter of Baby Boy Doe' (123 Idaho 464 (1993) and 127 Idaho 452 (1995)) are successive appeals in the same case, referred to internally as Doe I and Doe II. CourtListener titles the 1993 cluster 'Indian Tribe v. Doe' and the 1995 cluster 'Doe v. Roe'; both are duplicated in CourtListener under additional clusters (1135579 and 2607111) carrying the same reporter citations.

ICWA gaps: no Idaho appellate decision was found on transfer of a state child-custody proceeding to tribal court under 25 U.S.C. s 1911(b), on good cause to depart from s 1915 placement preferences, or on the qualified-expert-witness requirement as an independent holding. Coeur d'Alene Tribe v. Johnson, 162 Idaho 754, 405 P.3d 13 (2017), surfaced in the ICWA search but concerns recognition of a tribal land judgment and is not on point; it is excluded.

IDHW v. John Doe (2023-25), No. 50875 (Idaho Nov. 3, 2023), carries no reporter citation in CourtListener and is cited here in slip form. It is a published, signed opinion of the Idaho Supreme Court (Bevan, C.J.), not an unpublished memorandum, and it is the only retrieved authority addressing the standard of proof at a redisposition hearing under I.C. s 16-1623. Verify the parallel P.3d citation before filing.
No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used anywhere in this brief. All thirty-five cases are marked Published in CourtListener.

FAIL-03 and all six PMC nodes have no Idaho case law. Suter v. Artist M. and Blessing v. Freestone are the governing federal standard and are given as such: Title IV-E and IV-B state-plan conditions, including reasonable efforts and substantial-compliance requirements of the kind the CFSR measures, are not privately enforceable, which is precisely why accountability for them runs through federal administrative review, audit, and public disclosure rather than litigation. Henry A. v. Willden marks the narrow set of Child Welfare Act provisions that survive that rule in this circuit.

Turner v. Turner is a Domestic Violence Crime Prevention Act case rather than a CPA case. It is mapped to ACT-05 because Idaho protective orders restraining contact with a child issue under the DVCPA (I.C. s 39-6301 et seq.), as Davidson v. Davidson also illustrates.

D.A.F. v. Lieteau arises from the Department of Juvenile Corrections rather than foster care, but it is the Idaho Supreme Court's controlling holding on ITCA notice for tort claims brought under the child-abuse claims statute, I.C. s 6-1701, and on the separate status of Idaho whistleblower claims. It is the closest Idaho authority to FAIL-04 and OUT-06; no Idaho appellate decision was found imposing liability for a child fatality occurring under CPS supervision.

FAIL-05: no Idaho appellate decision was found applying the Multiethnic Placement Act, the ADA, or the Idaho Human Rights Act to a foster or adoptive placement decision. Palmore v. Sidoti supplies the constitutional rule on race and placement; Patterson supplies Idaho's retaliation framework against the Department as an employer. A disability-based termination challenge under the ADA appears to be unaddressed in Idaho (a search for 'Americans with Disabilities Act' in both Idaho courts returned zero results).

Cover v. Idaho Board of Correction, No. 47004 (Idaho Nov. 20, 2020), was retrieved and read. It holds that an agency rule not promulgated as a Public Records Act exemption cannot support withholding and that a district court may not itself perform the interest-balancing the statute assigns to the agency. It is omitted from the case list only because it carries no reporter citation in CourtListener and duplicates Wade v. Taylor on the operative point; it is worth citing alongside Wade in any Idaho records dispute with the Department.

Practice point for FAIL-01: the two most common grounds on which Idaho child-protective appeals fail are not merits-based. IDHW v. John Doe and Jane Doe (2023-22) shows dismissal for a missed briefing deadline notwithstanding the expedited nature of these appeals, and John Doe v. Jane Doe (2018) shows that stipulating to a disposition at the hearing forfeits appellate review of it entirely.

Missing (for a later pass): Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Hays, 137 Idaho 233, 46 P.3d 529 (2002) — the actual source of the rule the brief quotes from In re Adoption of John Doe ('The Department has the sole authority to withhold its permission from the prospective adoptive parents'); In re Adoption of John Doe cites Hays for it. A brief relying on the Department-consent prerequisite for ACT-04, OUT-02 and OUT-03 should cite the originating holding, not only the 2011 application.

Missing (for a later pass): Roe Family Services v. Doe, 139 Idaho 930, 88 P.3d 749 (2004) — repeatedly relied on by the Idaho Supreme Court in State v. Doe and Doe (2016-14) both as the case where 'a magistrate judge failed to apply the correct law to the facts in a termination case' and as the source of Idaho's longstanding presumption that a natural parent should have custody. It is a leading FAIL-01 and OUT-01 authority and is absent.

Missing (for a later pass): Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe, 151 Idaho 498, 260 P.3d 1169 (2011) — the decision IDHW v. Jane Doe (2019) relies on to reject the argument that the CPA's reasonable-efforts duty conditions a termination petition; it holds that once the parent stipulates to CPA jurisdiction and custody is vested, the Department may petition under I.C. Sec. 16-1624. Foundational for ACT-02 and OUT-01 and absent from the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of Doe Children, 164 Idaho 486, 432 P.3d 35 (2018) — quoted inside IDHW v. John Doe (2023-25) as the current statement that the State must prove at least one statutory ground and best interests by clear and convincing evidence. It is the cleanest recent Idaho articulation of the two-part termination test and would anchor DEC-03 and OUT-02 better than Santosky alone.

Missing (for a later pass): Ellibee v. Ellibee, 121 Idaho 501, 826 P.2d 462 (1992) — the decision Turner v. Turner expressly declines to disturb and the actual origin of the preponderance-of-the-evidence burden under the Domestic Violence Crime Prevention Act. Citing Turner for the DVCPA standard without Ellibee cites the reaffirmance rather than the holding (ACT-05).

Missing (for a later pass): Van v. Portneuf Medical Center, 147 Idaho 552, 212 P.3d 982 (2009) — the case that actually holds an Idaho whistleblower claim is a statutory action not subject to the ITCA notice requirement. The brief misattributes that holding to D.A.F. v. Lieteau, which merely discusses and distinguishes Van. Required for FAIL-05 and FAIL-06.

Missing (for a later pass): Bolger v. Lance, 137 Idaho 792, 53 P.3d 1211 (2002) — cited in Wade v. Taylor for the rule that the entity withholding records bears the burden of demonstrating that they are exempt. It is the burden-allocation authority a records requester needs alongside Wade (PMC-05, FAIL-06).

Missing (for a later pass): Federated Publications, Inc. v. Boise City, 128 Idaho 459, 915 P.2d 21 (1996) — cited in Wade v. Taylor for the presumption that all public records are open unless expressly exempted and for narrow construction of exemptions. The foundational Idaho Public Records Act case and absent (PMC-05, INP-09).

Missing (for a later pass): State v. Pearson-Anderson, 136 Idaho 847, 41 P.3d 275 (Ct. App. 2001) — the decision State v. Barrett quotes for Idaho's exigency test ('compelling need for official action and no time to secure a warrant') and for the risk-of-danger-to-persons-inside formulation. If the brief is going to rely on Idaho's own emergency-aid rule for INP-12 and DEC-04, it should cite the case Barrett applies.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-20): all nine authorities named by the verifier in the nine 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above were located in CourtListener by reporter citation, their clusters and opinions retrieved, their opinion text read, and all nine confirmed real, Published, and on point. None failed verification; there is no unverifiable authority to report. The nine 'Missing' notes immediately above are retained for provenance but are now RESOLVED — each of those cases appears in the cases array and in node_map.

Added Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Hays, 137 Idaho 233, 46 P.3d 529 (2002) (cluster 2637019) for ACT-04, OUT-02 and OUT-03: it is the originating Idaho holding that the Department, as post-termination guardian, is the only entity whose consent to adoption is required and therefore selects the adoptive parents; In re Adoption of John Doe (2011) is an application of it. The opinion also fixes the annual future-status hearing obligation under I.C. s 16-2010(c) until a permanent placement exists.

Added Roe Family Services v. Doe, 139 Idaho 930, 88 P.3d 749 (2004) (cluster 2572495) for FAIL-01 and OUT-01: it is the Idaho Supreme Court's canonical statement that findings can be supported by substantial and competent evidence and the termination still reversed for application of the wrong law, and it reverses a termination taken without notice to an acknowledged biological father, directing custody and visitation to him.

Added Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe, 151 Idaho 498, 260 P.3d 1169 (2011) (cluster 5342134) for ACT-02, OUT-01, DEC-05 and FAIL-05: it holds that I.C. s 16-1624 authorizes a termination petition as soon as the court finds CPA jurisdiction and vests custody or protective supervision, so an incomplete case plan is no bar; it separately holds that the Department has no duty to notify a parent that she qualifies as disabled, the parent's statutory right being to offer adaptive-equipment and supportive-services evidence — the closest Idaho authority on disability in a termination, which the FAIL-05 note above had recorded as absent.

Added Idaho Dep't of Health & Welfare v. Doe (In Re Doe), 164 Idaho 486, 432 P.3d 35 (2018) (cluster 4575190) — the decision the verifier calls 'Matter of Doe Children' — for DEC-03 and OUT-02: it states the current Idaho two-part termination test (a statutory ground plus best interests, each by clear and convincing evidence) in the court's own words, anchoring those nodes in Idaho law rather than in Santosky alone.

Added Ellibee v. Ellibee, 121 Idaho 501, 826 P.2d 462 (1992) (cluster 1250040) for ACT-05: it is the originating Idaho holding that the DVCPA reaches protection orders in favour of children even against a joint legal custodian and that the burden of proof is preponderance of the evidence — the holding Turner v. Turner later declines to disturb.

Added Van v. Portneuf Medical Center, 147 Idaho 552, 212 P.3d 982 (2009) (cluster 874358) for FAIL-05, FAIL-06 and PMC-05: it is the actual holding that an Idaho whistleblower claim is a purely statutory remedy not subject to the ITCA notice requirement. The earlier note correctly flagged that the brief had misattributed this to D.A.F. v. Lieteau; D.A.F. remains in the brief for its own holding (ITCA notice DOES apply to tort claims under I.C. s 6-1701), and Van now supplies the whistleblower half.

Added Bolger v. Lance, 137 Idaho 792, 53 P.3d 1211 (2002) (cluster 2581839) for PMC-05, FAIL-06, INP-09 and PMC-02: it is the burden-allocation authority Wade v. Taylor relies on — the withholding agency must show cause and prove that each record fits a narrowly construed exemption — while also showing that in camera review of the documents themselves can satisfy that burden and that the investigatory-records exemption reaches only ongoing investigations.

Added Federated Publications, Inc. v. Boise City, 128 Idaho 459, 915 P.2d 21 (1996) (cluster 1310352) for PMC-05, INP-09, FAIL-06 and PMC-06: it is the foundational Idaho Public Records Act decision establishing the presumption of openness and narrow construction of exemptions, and it holds that an agency's internal administrative review of its own personnel's conduct is not automatically an exempt personnel record — directly useful against a categorical child-welfare refusal. The quote is from the majority's Part III; Justice Schroeder's partial dissent is not relied on.

Added State v. Pearson-Anderson, 136 Idaho 847, 41 P.3d 275 (Ct. App. 2001) (cluster 2600824) for INP-12, DEC-04, INP-03 and ACT-06: it is the decision State v. Barrett applies for Idaho's exigency test, and it states in the court's own words that a warrantless home entry is presumptively unlawful absent a recognised exception, while upholding a brief entry to look for a third person who might need help after a 911 hang-up. The quote is from the majority; Judge Lansing's Buie-based special concurrence is not relied on.

node_map reconciliation: the prior node_map was a curated subset of the per-case relevance objects and left five nodes (INP-04, INP-07, DEC-01, ACT-01, OUT-05) mapped to a single case even though other cases in the brief already carried relevance sentences for them. Those five were reconciled from the existing relevance objects (INP-04 gains Roe v. State and Wood v. State; INP-07 gains Wallis v. Spencer; DEC-01 gains Davidson and Mabe; ACT-01 gains IDHW v. Jane Doe (2019); OUT-05 gains IDHW v. John Doe and Jane Doe (2023-22) and John Doe v. Jane Doe (2018)). Every one of the 42 nodes now carries between 2 and 6 cases.

OUT-02 curation: nine cases in this brief carry an OUT-02 relevance sentence, which exceeds the six-case ceiling for a node. The six listed in node_map are the ones a practitioner should cite first — Santosky (federal floor), Lassiter (counsel floor), Doe (2014-09) (best interests as an independent element), Doe (2014-26) (incarceration ground), Hays (Department consent) and In Re Doe, 164 Idaho 486 (the current two-part test). In re Adoption of John Doe (874174), Baby Boy Doe (5341698), Doe (2013-15) (2657054), IDHW v. Doe, 161 Idaho 596 (4255320), Jane (2014-23) Doe (3133269) and State v. Doe (874513) retain their OUT-02 relevance sentences and are each mapped at other nodes.

Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe, 151 Idaho 498, 260 P.3d 1169 (2011) appears in CourtListener under two clusters: 5342134 (carrying both the Idaho Reports and P.3d citations, opinion id 5174767, used here) and 874107 (P.3d only). Resolve by cluster 5342134.

Gap searches run in this pass that produced nothing new: INP-07 (Medical Disclosure) — searches of both Idaho courts for a decision on physician reporting, hospital disclosure, or an investigatory medical examination of a child returned no on-point published authority beyond Davidson v. Davidson; the node remains served by Davidson and by Wallis v. Spencer's Ninth Circuit rule on examinations of a seized child. FAIL-04 and PMC-04 — searches for a child fatality or a death in foster care in either Idaho court returned nothing; those nodes remain served by DeShaney, Henry A. v. Willden and D.A.F. v. Lieteau, and no Idaho fatality-review decision exists. INP-06 (Anonymous Tip / Hotline) — searches for anonymous reporting or hotline intake in either Idaho court returned nothing; the node remains served by Davidson (bad-faith reporting) and Wallis (uncorroborated tip cannot supply reasonable cause). A query for 'mandatory reporter' as a phrase returns zero results in both Idaho courts; the reporting case law is reachable only through the statute numbers (I.C. s 16-1605 et seq.).

Counts after this pass: 42 distinct cases; 32 Idaho (26 Idaho Supreme Court, 6 Idaho Court of Appeals... corrected: 5 Idaho Court of Appeals — Davidson, Barrett, Wood, Pearson-Anderson), 4 Ninth Circuit and 6 U.S. Supreme Court. All 42 are marked Published in CourtListener. Every quote added in this pass was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after normalizing whitespace and curly quotation marks, is 30 words or fewer, and was confirmed to sit in the majority opinion body.

Missing (for a later pass): Kirkpatrick v. County of Washoe, 843 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 2016) (en banc) — the brief's own Fourth Amendment note names 'the en banc Kirkpatrick' as part of the governing law for Idaho actors, but it appears nowhere in the cases array or node_map. It is the current en banc statement of the warrantless-removal/exigency rule and post-dates Wallis, Mabe and Rogers; a brief relying on those three at DEC-04, FAIL-02 and INP-12 without the en banc decision that refined them is citing superseded formulations.

Missing (for a later pass): Gonzaga University v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002) — the controlling test for when a federal statute creates a right enforceable under s 1983, decided after Blessing and expressly tightening it. FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02 and PMC-03 all rest on Suter and Blessing alone; an opponent will point out that Gonzaga now supplies the governing framework and that Henry A. applies Gonzaga, not Blessing in isolation.

Missing (for a later pass): Stockwell v. Stockwell, 116 Idaho 297, 775 P.2d 611 (1989) — confirmed to exist and quoted at length in Roe Family Services v. Doe (cluster 2572495). It is the origin of Idaho's presumption that a natural parent should have custody as against a non-parent, and of the rule that the presumption precludes consideration of best interests unless abandonment, unfitness or appreciable-period custody is shown. OUT-01, OUT-03 and INP-05 currently cite the applications (State v. Doe, Roe Family Services, Copenhaver) without the holding.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — the federal constitutional foundation for an unwed biological father's right to notice and a hearing before his children are taken. It is the doctrinal backdrop to Roe Family Services v. Doe, which the brief has now added for FAIL-01 and OUT-01, and it is absent.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the leading modern Supreme Court statement of the fundamental liberty interest of fit parents in the care, custody and control of their children, and of the deference owed a fit parent's decisions. Routinely cited in Idaho guardianship and third-party custody litigation; directly supports Copenhaver at OUT-03 and the INP-05 analysis, and appears nowhere in the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) — the foundational Supreme Court ICWA decision on domicile and exclusive tribal jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. s 1911(a). INP-11 rests entirely on the two Idaho Baby Boy Doe appeals and Jane (2014-23) Doe with no federal ICWA authority at all.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) — narrows 25 U.S.C. ss 1912(d) and 1912(f) where the parent never had custody, and is the decision most often deployed against the active-efforts and beyond-a-reasonable-doubt requirements the brief relies on at INP-11 and ACT-03. Its absence leaves the ICWA nodes stating the pre-2013 position without the qualification a court will apply.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — rejects the constitutional challenges to ICWA and is the current word on the statute's validity and on who may raise equal-protection objections to the s 1915 placement preferences. An ICWA-heavy brief verified in 2026 that stops at 2015 Idaho authority is materially out of date at INP-11 and ACT-04.

Missing (for a later pass): Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) — the brief's DEC-03 note observes that no Idaho decision applies a Mathews challenge to a substantiated finding, but then omits Mathews itself. It is the framework any due-process challenge to an agency substantiation or central-registry listing must be built on, and DEC-03 currently has no authority addressing the administrative finding at all.
